Text: The system of units most important in physics today is abbreviated SI, which stands for {{c1::Système International::its French name}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: in English, Système International is "International System."

Distinguish: SI is not the only system of units in use — the cgs system and the British engineering system are two others.

Text: The system of units now known as the SI used to be called the {{c1::MKS::acronym}} system.
Back Extra:
Meaning: MKS stands for meter-kilogram-second — the SI's standards of length, mass, and time, in that order.

Distinguish: MKS and cgs are both metric systems, but MKS builds on the meter and kilogram while cgs builds on the centimeter and gram.

Text: The British engineering system's standards are the foot for length, the second for time, and the pound for {{c1::force::force/mass}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the metric systems standardize mass in that slot — the kilogram in SI, the gram in cgs — while the British engineering system standardizes a force.

Cue: the British engineering system is used more in the U.S. than in Britain.

Pitfall: the SI is not just the meter, second, and kilogram — those cover only length, time, and mass, and four more base quantities round out the set.
